t: 3656 — Determine if a Simple Graph Exists
o: Decide whether a degree sequence is graphical. The classical answer is the Erdős–Gallai theorem: the degree sum must be even, and for every k, the sum of the k largest degrees must not exceed k(k−1) (edges inside the top set) plus Σ min(dᵢ, k) over the rest (edges crossing the cut). With sorting and prefix sums plus binary search for the min-terms, all k checks run in O(n log n).
k: Necessary: total degree must be even (handshake lemma).
Erdős–Gallai: for each k, sum of k largest degrees ≤ k(k−1) + Σ_{rest} min(dᵢ, k).
Sorted degrees + prefix sums + binary search evaluate each min-term in O(log n).

a.i: Sort degrees ascending with prefix sums P. For each k, the LHS is the sum of the k largest = P[n] − P[n−k]. For the RHS, among the first n−k degrees, those exceeding k contribute k each and the rest contribute themselves; binary search finds the split point. Checking all k verifies graphicality by the theorem.
s: If the degree sum is odd, return false.
Sort ascending, build prefix sums P.
For k = 1..n: LHS = P[n] − P[n−k]; let j = count of the first n−k degrees that are ≤ k (bisect). RHS = k(k−1) + k·((n−k) − j) + P[j].
If any LHS > RHS, return false; otherwise true.
a.t: O(n log n) — sort plus n binary searches
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy and prefix sums

a.i: Repeatedly take the vertex of largest degree d, 'connect' it to the d next-largest vertices (decrement their degrees), and reinsert. If d exceeds the remaining vertex count, or any degree goes negative, no simple graph exists. This constructive algorithm is easier to explain but runs in O(n² log n), fine conceptually, risky at n = 1e5.
s: Heapify negated degrees; check the sum is even.
Pop the max d; if d > heap size, return false.
Decrement the next d largest; if any drops below 0, return false; push them back.
If the heap empties cleanly, return true.
a.t: O(n² log n) — each round pops up to d elements; fine for exposition, slow at n = 1e5

w: Always lead with Erdős–Gallai for the constraints given; Havel–Hakimi is the intuitive teaching version and doubles as a way to construct an explicit graph if asked. Pitfalls: forgetting the parity check (EG implies it via k=n only partially — actually k=n gives sum ≤ n(n−1), so the explicit even-sum check is required), 64-bit sums (degrees up to 1e5 × 1e5), and off-by-one in the binary-search split point.
